newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Serbs are outcasts in their former homes.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Serbs are outcasts in their former homes.

text.p: Sava Strbac returned to his Croatian village after years of working in Germany to find his fellow Serbs there had become a segregated minority, oppressed by people he had never seen.

But for the neighbours who took him in, Strbac, 54, would be a homeless outcast, sharing the fate of some dozen Serb families who recently returned to Kistanje but have been denied the right to live in their houses.

Kistanje was once a prosperous Serb village, sprawling across a plain in southern Croatia. Now it is run by ethnic Croats from Yugoslavia's province of Kosovo, where they were a minority for centuries.
They have been moving in at Croatia's invitation because the village was abandoned when government troops reconquered the Serb region of Krajina in 1995.
Benny Otim, head of the U.N. refugee office in the nearby town of Knin, summed up the problem on Thursday:

"Most Serb houses in Kistanje were empty, so the owners came back and moved in, with approval from the police. But last week, in total disregard of the agreement (on the return of refugees), government representatives told them to leave."
"No explanation, no advice on alternative accommodation was given and the houses were sealed," he said, adding that about 100 Croat families from Kosovo had arrived so far.

Croatia has promised safety to Serbs wishing to go back to their pre-war homes but many are finding their houses occupied by Croat refugees from other parts of former Yugoslavia, or destroyed. Before the war around half a million ethnic Serbs lived in Croatia, now around 100,000 remain.
Zagreb insists all displaced people have the right to return home but the returns must be properly organised.
Strbac, having obtained all necessary Croatian citizenship and property documents, came back to Kistanje from Germany on May 2. His house was badly burned but still standing.
"A few days later those Croats told me to leave the house. I assume it was reserved for one of them. The next day they forbade my wife to work in our vineyard.

"Now the house is empty, it is not being reconstructed and I can't go back in. If I had been in the war and harmed someone, I would understand. But now it looks like I've worked all my life to build this house for nothing," he said bitterly.
Branimir Radev of the OSCE office in Knin confirmed the government had encouraged Kosovo Croats to come here "in order to repopulate the empty village".
"Obviously those Croats didn't feel secure in Kosovo and they have a right to live somewhere. But the Serbs are citizens of Croatia and also have a right to return," Radev said.

Another Western official in the area said temporary confiscation of Serb houses was "a flagrant violation of property rights, based on legislation". Croatia has passed a law allowing the temporary occupation of Serb property.
The new residents of Kistanje have set about rebuilding the village. Although loathe to speak to journalists, they admit they are receiving substantial aid in basic household supplies.

"We are happy to be here because life for Croats in Kosovo was hell. We're finally in our own country but we are once again worrying about what will happen if all Serbs return," said a waiter in the village cafe.
"This is infinitely better than Kosovo," he said.

Milka Bjelanovic, a Serb who stayed in the village after the war, said even the Croatian army troops treated the Serbs better than the newcomers did. "When the Croatian army passed here in 1995, they sat down and had a drink with me," she said.
"These people won't even talk to us, they only issue orders and steal everything they can lay their hands on," added her husband Luka.
